title: Death poems
hookLine: the short verse a Zen teacher leaves at the end of life

lines: A FEW LINES, THEN THE BRUSH GOES DOWN.
cards: A brush, an ink stone and a sheet of paper beside a sickbed. In a Zen temple, an old teacher is near the end, and the students have gathered. Someone grinds the ink.
Someone asks, quietly, whether there will be a verse. The teacher writes a few lines, sometimes only a handful of words: the moon, snow on a branch, a breath, even a joke. Then the brush goes down.
Zen and Chan tradition kept these short verses and passed them on with the teaching. Today: death poems.

teach.h: JISEI: A FAREWELL TO THE WORLD.
teach.b: First, the custom. In Japanese a death poem is jisei, a farewell to the world. Tradition says Chan and Zen teachers were asked for one as the end came near, and their students copied the verses down and kept them.
They're short. Some are calm, some fierce, some funny. Stories are also told of teachers who refused to write one at all, as if the whole life had already been the poem.
Second, an older echo. Some readers hear one in the Pali suttas.

In the sutta on the Buddha's last days, his final words are short too. In Rhys Davids' translation: "Decay is inherent in all component things! Work out your salvation with diligence!" Not a farewell about himself.
A last teaching, for the people who would still be alive tomorrow. Third, what a death poem does. It isn't a will or a list of achievements.
Zen teachers spent their lives pointing at this moment: the bowl, the breath, the cypress in the garden.
A death poem points at the last moment the same way, so its subjects are plain things: a cloud, a bird, morning light, empty hands. Fourth, why it belongs on an ordinary day.
It asks: what is worth saying last?
The answer can be small, a window, a name, a cup of tea. The custom doesn't ask for gloom. It asks for attention, while there's still a brush in the hand.

how: In Chan and Zen tradition, teachers near death have traditionally been asked for a short verse, called jisei in Japanese, which students wrote down and kept alongside the teacher's other words.

o: poems a student writes when leaving the temple
short verses Zen teachers left at the end of life
prayers chanted over the dead at a Zen funeral

p: plain things: a cloud, a bird

s: a death poem has to be solemn
tradition keeps calm ones, fierce ones and funny ones.
the Buddha's last words were a teaching for those still alive
"work out your salvation with diligence," in Rhys Davids' translation.
no Zen teacher ever refused to write one
stories are told of teachers who refused, as if the whole life had been the poem.

games.q: you're the old teacher. the students have ground the ink and are waiting. what goes on the paper?
o: a long account of everything you achieved.
a few plain lines: the moon, a breath, snow on a branch.
a list of rules for running the temple.
games.why: death poems are short and point at plain things. a death poem is one more act of seeing clearly, not a will or a résumé.

practice: With a pen or just in your mind, make four short lines, no rules, no rhyme: something you can see right now, something you can hear, one person or thing you're glad of, and anything at all, or nothing.
It isn't a goodbye; it's a look around, so sit still afterward and breathe with whatever you made.
If thinking about endings ever brings up more than you can carry, or you don't want to be alive, please call or text 988 in the US, or reach local emergency help.

wordCard.voice: Death poems. In Japanese, jisei: a short verse left at the end of life in Chan and Zen tradition, usually pointing at something plain and close at hand. Today's word.

orig.note: Japanese: jisei, a farewell to the world. a death poem is also called jisei no ku (辞世の句).

carryVoice: Your line: a last poem. Plain things, seen clearly, right to the end. Until tomorrow.
